intro:
The exercises in this chapter all circle one discipline: turning vague confidence about a pointer or a chunk of memory into a written list of preconditions, and then placing the unsafe operation behind a boundary that makes those preconditions true before the operation runs. You start by naming invariants in prose, move to spotting where a real routine leaves obligations undocumented, then implement a safe wrapper over an unsafe internal write, repair a MaybeUninit ordering bug, decide honestly whether an API should be safe or unsafe, and finally design an FFI adapter that converts C contracts into Rust types.

The through-line is the containment boundary from the chapter: almost everything is ordinary safe Rust where the compiler proves memory safety, and a small explicit region holds the operations the compiler cannot prove. Your job in every exercise is to keep that region small, attach a precise SAFETY justification, and make sure each check that legitimizes the unsafe step already holds by the time control reaches it.

exerciseSolutions.title: Name the invariant before the pointer
exerciseSolutions.solution:
slice::from_raw_parts(ptr, len) does not validate anything. It trusts you. So the invariants must be stated as caller obligations, not as runtime checks the function performs.

Pointer validity. The pointer must be non-null. from_raw_parts specifically forbids a null pointer even when len is 0; in that case it still requires a non-null, properly aligned dangling pointer such as NonNull::dangling(). It must be aligned to align_of::<u8>() (trivially 1 for bytes, but for a typed parser returning a wider element type alignment matters). The entire range ptr..ptr.add(len) must point into a single allocated object that is currently live, and all len elements must be initialized and readable. The total size len * size_of::<T>() must not exceed isize::MAX, which is what keeps pointer arithmetic from wrapping.

Lifetime story. from_raw_parts produces &'a [u8] for some lifetime 'a that the caller chooses, and nothing ties that 'a to the real owner of the backing allocation. The invariant is that the backing memory must remain valid and unmoved for the entire span of 'a, and the produced slice must not outlive the packet buffer it was carved from. If the parser's buffer is dropped, reallocated (a Vec growing), or reused while the slice is still reachable, the slice dangles. The honest practice is to bound 'a to the borrow of the owner, for example by writing a function whose signature already ties the output lifetime to an input &Buffer.

Aliasing story. A shared slice &[u8] asserts that for its whole lifetime nothing mutates the bytes it covers. If you also hold a *mut into the same region and write through it, that is a violation even though no &mut exists, because the optimizer is allowed to assume the &[u8] data is immutable. If instead you build &mut [u8] via from_raw_parts_mut, the requirement is stronger: that range must be exclusively yours, with no other live reference or other mutable pointer reading or writing it for the slice's lifetime. Aliasing is the rule that turns a merely-readable pointer into a valid reference.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The safe form lets the slice API enforce bounds and lifetime; the raw form must spell the same facts out as an unsafe contract.
criteria: Pointer validity is named explicitly: non-null even at len 0, aligned, and all len elements live and readable inside one allocation.
The lifetime obligation is stated: the slice cannot outlive the owner of the backing buffer, and is upheld by tying 'a to &self.
Aliasing is addressed for both cases: a shared slice forbids concurrent mutation, and a mutable slice requires exclusive access to the range.

exerciseSolutions.title: Find the UB risks in a raw-pointer copy helper
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The function under review looks like a thin memcpy: it takes dst: *mut u8, src: *const u8, len: usize, loops with pointer arithmetic, and is exposed as a safe pub fn with no checks. The defect is not that it uses raw pointers; it is that it makes promises it cannot keep. A safe function asserts that no input can cause undefined behavior, but this function can do nothing to make that true, because every fact it depends on lives in the caller.

Undocumented caller obligations. There are several, not one. (1) Non-null: both dst and src must be non-null; the loop dereferences them with no guard. (2) Validity for the range: src must be readable for len bytes and dst must be writable for len bytes, each within a single live allocation. (3) Writability: dst must point to memory the caller is actually allowed to write, not into a read-only mapping or a shorter buffer. (4) Bounds: len must not exceed either allocation; nothing checks this. (5) Aliasing and overlap: if src and dst regions overlap, a byte-by-byte forward copy may corrupt data, which is the classic memcpy-versus-memmove distinction; more fundamentally, holding both a *mut and a *const into overlapping ranges and writing is an aliasing question. (6) Lifetime: both allocations must stay live and unmoved for the whole call. (7) Initialization: src bytes must be initialized, or you propagate uninitialized memory. None of these appear as documentation or as runtime checks.

Should it stay safe? No. A safe public API is wrong precisely because the callee cannot enforce the contract. The function cannot test whether a raw *mut u8 is valid for len writes; that information simply is not recoverable from a bare address at runtime. Marking it safe is a lie that the borrow checker will faithfully propagate, letting safe callers invoke undefined behavior without an unsafe block anywhere in sight. The two honest options are: make it unsafe fn with a written contract enumerating the obligations above, so callers must acknowledge them at the call site; or redesign it around slices so the obligations become statically checked. The slice redesign is strongly preferred for anything that does not cross an FFI boundary, because &[u8] and &mut [u8] carry length, validity, initialization, exclusivity, and lifetime as part of the type, and the standard copy_from_slice already encodes the overlap-safe, length-matched copy.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Option B moves every obligation into the type system; Option A at least relocates the obligation to the caller's unsafe block instead of hiding it.
criteria: Multiple distinct obligations are identified: non-null, range validity, writability, bounds, overlap/aliasing, lifetime, and initialization.
The safe public signature is explained as wrong because the callee cannot validate a bare raw pointer at runtime, so safety would be asserted falsely.
Both remedies are offered: an unsafe fn with a documented SAFETY contract, and a slice-based redesign that makes the obligations static.

exerciseSolutions.title: Wrap unsafe internals in a safe public API
exerciseSolutions.solution:
This is the canonical shape of a safe abstraction over unsafe internals: validate the precondition first, and only then enter a small unsafe block that inherits an already-proven invariant. The public signature stays safe because the function can fully enforce its own contract. It receives &mut [u8], which carries both the length (so bounds are checkable) and exclusive access (so no aliasing write can race it), and it returns a Result so the one failure mode it cares about is expressed in the type rather than as a panic or silent corruption.

The length check is the load-bearing line. Buffers shorter than four bytes return Err("buffer too small") before any pointer is formed. Once control passes that early return, the four writes at offsets 0..4 are guaranteed in-bounds, so ptr.add(3).write(33) cannot stray outside the allocation. The bytes 82, 83, 84, 33 are the ASCII codes for R, S, T, and !, so a valid buffer reads RST! when interpreted as UTF-8.

Why the unsafe block is justified, in the chapter's terms: the only genuinely unsafe step is pointer arithmetic plus write, and everything around it exists to make that one step legal. The exclusive &mut [u8] borrow supplies the aliasing guarantee, the length check supplies the bounds guarantee, and u8 has no drop glue, so overwriting the existing bytes with .write() does not skip a destructor. Note that for a drop-carrying element type such as String, using .write() over an already-initialized slot would leak the old value's resources, and you would reach for std::ptr::drop_in_place or simple assignment instead. For u8 the write method is exactly right.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The early return makes the precondition true before the unsafe block runs, so the four raw writes inherit a proven bounds-and-exclusivity invariant.
criteria: Buffers shorter than four bytes return Err("buffer too small") via the early return before any pointer is formed.
Buffers of length four or more return Ok(()) and contain 82, 83, 84, 33, which decode to RST!.
The unsafe region is four writes only, and it executes solely after the length check has established the bounds invariant.

exerciseSolutions.title: Move `assume_init` to the only valid place
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The inherited code does this: MaybeUninit::<[u32; 4]>::uninit(), then assume_init() immediately, then writes only some elements into the resulting array. The one-sentence explanation for a reviewer: assume_init is called while the storage is still uninitialized, so the program claims a valid [u32; 4] exists and then reads or moves uninitialized memory as if it were a real typed value, which is undefined behavior.

Where writes must occur. Every initialization write must happen through the MaybeUninit storage, before assume_init, not after it. assume_init is not a constructor and performs no work at runtime; it is a promise to the compiler that the bytes already hold a valid T. The correct order is a one-way ratchet: start in the not-yet-valid state, write every element exactly once into the uninitialized storage, and only at the end assert validity. What must be true before the final [u32; 4] exists is that all four u32 slots have been written; only then does every invariant of the type hold and the value legitimately exists.

The repair is about order, not about adding more unsafe. The fix keeps a single small unsafe block, writes all four elements into the MaybeUninit, and moves assume_init to be the last operation, after the loop completes. A common and even safer variant avoids the raw cast entirely by treating the storage as [MaybeUninit<u32>; 4] and writing element by element, then transmuting once everything is initialized; for an array of a Copy type like u32, simply building the value directly without MaybeUninit at all is the most honest option when the elements are known up front. MaybeUninit earns its place only when you genuinely cannot produce all elements before you need typed storage, for example when initializing in place to avoid an extra copy on a hot path.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: assume_init moves to the final position, after all four slots are written; before that point the storage is not a valid array.
criteria: The value stays inside MaybeUninit storage and every element is written through that storage before any assume_init.
assume_init is the last operation, executed only once full initialization is complete.
The bug is explained as reading uninitialized memory as a valid [u32; 4], which treats invalid bytes as a typed value.

exerciseSolutions.title: Decide whether the function should be safe or unsafe
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The function fn view<'a>(ptr: *const u8, len: usize) -> &'a [u8] is unsound as a safe function and should not exist in that form. The fatal flaw is the unconstrained lifetime parameter 'a. Because 'a appears only in the return type and is not tied to any input, the caller may freely choose 'a = 'static, and the function will happily manufacture a 'static slice out of a pointer to a buffer that lives for one stack frame. The callee cannot verify the pointer is valid for an arbitrary 'a, because validity-for-a-lifetime is a fact about the lifetime of the backing allocation, and a bare *const u8 carries no such information. The function is asserting a lifetime it cannot prove.

Is the returned lifetime tied to a real owner? No, and that is the whole problem. A reference's lifetime is supposed to be a conservative under-approximation of how long the referent is valid. Here the lifetime is invented at the call site with no connection to the owner of the bytes, so the type system's central guarantee, that a live reference always points to live memory, is silently broken. This is the lifetime fiction the chapter warns about: raw pointers plus arbitrary returned references are exactly where it becomes dangerous.

The honest redesign. There are three coherent shapes, in order of preference. (1) If a borrowed view is wanted, take the source as &[u8] (or a wrapper that owns the bytes) and return a sub-slice; the borrow checker then ties the output lifetime to a real owner with no unsafe at all. (2) If the bytes truly come from a raw source such as FFI, make it unsafe fn view<'a>(ptr: *const u8, len: usize) -> &'a [u8] with a SAFETY contract stating that the caller must guarantee the pointer is valid and initialized for len bytes and that 'a does not exceed the real lifetime of the backing allocation; this relocates the obligation to the caller, who has the context to discharge it. (3) If the data should be owned downstream, return Vec<u8> by copying, eliminating the lifetime question entirely. The distinction throughout is between caller-held obligations, which an unsafe fn makes explicit, and callee-enforced checks, which a safe slice-based signature lets the compiler verify.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The unconstrained 'a is the defect; the three fixes either tie the lifetime to an owner, make the obligation an unsafe contract, or remove the lifetime by owning the data.
criteria: It is explained that the callee cannot manufacture an arbitrary valid lifetime, because validity-for-'a is a property of the backing allocation that a raw pointer does not carry.
A concrete more-honest API is proposed: a borrowed &[u8] view, an unsafe fn with a SAFETY contract, or an owned Vec<u8> return.
Caller-held obligations (made explicit by unsafe fn) are distinguished from callee-enforced checks (provided by a safe slice signature).

exerciseSolutions.title: Wrap an FFI boundary without exporting C mistakes
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The design principle is a single translation layer with one direction of travel. Unsafe lives in exactly one adapter module, not in every caller. Raw C values, *const c_char error strings and *mut Record results, enter that module, are converted into Rust types that carry the guarantee, and from there inward the entire service, the parser, the retry loop, the request handlers, is ordinary safe Rust that never touches a raw pointer. If application code anywhere outside the adapter still manipulates *mut Record, the boundary is too wide and the C mistakes have leaked into the system.

Translating the three C contracts into Rust types. Nullability becomes Option or, more usefully, an early conversion to Result: a returned *mut Record that may be null maps to Option<NonNull<Record>>, and a null result combined with a non-null error string maps to Err. Ownership transfer becomes an owned newtype with a Drop impl. If the C library hands back a *mut Record that the caller must later free with record_free, wrap it in a struct Record(NonNull<ffi::Record>) whose Drop calls record_free exactly once; this makes the resource releasable only through the safe owner and prevents double-free and leak by construction. The borrowed-versus-owned distinction matters: a Record we must free is owned; a *const Record the library still owns and only lends us for the duration of a call is a borrowed view with a lifetime no longer than that call. String validity becomes a checked conversion: a *const c_char is read via CStr::from_ptr inside unsafe (after a null check), then to_str() validates UTF-8 and yields Result, so invalid bytes surface as an error instead of propagating a malformed &str.

Cleanup and unwinding. Ownership of native resources rests with the Rust owner types, and release happens deterministically in their Drop, so the retry loop can drop a failed Record on each attempt without leaking. Two failure modes to call out: an error path that returns a null *const c_char (so the code must treat the error pointer itself as nullable, not assume a message exists), and a cleanup mismatch where a Record allocated by the C allocator is freed by the wrong deallocator, which is undefined behavior, so the Drop impl must call the library's own free function. On unwinding: a Rust panic must never cross back into C, because unwinding through a frame that is not prepared for it is undefined behavior. Any extern "C" callback the library invokes, or any closure run while C holds resources, should either use a panic-catching boundary (std::panic::catch_unwind) or be declared extern "C" so that on the abort-on-panic policy a panic aborts rather than unwinds into foreign frames. Stating that policy explicitly at the boundary is what keeps the unwinding assumptions from staying fuzzy.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: One adapter owns all unsafe: null becomes Result, ownership becomes a Drop newtype, and C string validity is checked via CStr::to_str before crossing inward.
criteria: All unsafe is confined to a single adapter module, and the rest of the service uses Result and owned types with no raw pointers.
Nullability maps to Option/Result, ownership transfer maps to a Drop-owning newtype, and C string validity maps to a checked CStr conversion.
Native resource ownership rests with the Rust Record type and release happens once in its Drop, with borrowed views distinguished from owned handles.
At least one failure mode is named: a null error pointer, invalid UTF-8 in the message, a mismatched free, or a panic unwinding across the C boundary.

labSolution.expectedOutput:
short = Err("buffer too small")
value = Ok(())
buf = RST!
labSolution.explanation:
The initial code is missing the one check that makes the unsafe writes legal: it dereferences four offsets without first confirming the buffer holds four bytes. The completed solution adds the early return if buf.len() < 4, which turns write_magic into a genuinely safe public function. For the three-byte buffer, control reaches the early return and the function yields Err("buffer too small") before any pointer is formed, so the first printed line is short = Err("buffer too small").

For the four-byte buffer, the length check passes, so the unsafe block runs with a proven invariant: offsets 0 through 3 are in-bounds, the &mut [u8] borrow guarantees exclusive access, and u8 carries no drop glue, so the four .write() calls are sound. The function returns Ok(()), giving value = Ok(()). The bytes written are 82, 83, 84, 33, the ASCII codes for R, S, T, and !, so std::str::from_utf8 over the now-filled buffer decodes to RST!, producing buf = RST!.

This is the chapter's safe-abstraction shape in miniature: a small unsafe core wrapped by a check that establishes its precondition, with a safe signature that callers can use without an unsafe block of their own.

reviewAnswers.question: What does an `unsafe` block let you do, and what does it not excuse?
reviewAnswers.answer: An unsafe block grants a specific, finite set of capabilities: dereferencing raw pointers, calling unsafe functions (including FFI), accessing or modifying mutable statics, implementing unsafe traits, and accessing union fields. It does not disable the borrow checker, type checking, ownership, or any ordinary Rust rule; the surrounding code still obeys them. Above all it does not excuse undefined behavior. unsafe simply means the compiler cannot prove this operation sound, so a human takes on the obligation to guarantee it, ideally recorded in a SAFETY comment.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is a data race undefined behavior in Rust rather than merely an unlucky concurrency bug?
reviewAnswers.answer: Rust's memory model, like C++'s, defines program behavior only for executions free of data races; an unsynchronized conflicting access (at least one a write) to the same location from two threads has no defined meaning at all. Because the behavior is undefined rather than merely nondeterministic, the optimizer is entitled to assume it cannot happen and may reorder, cache, or eliminate accesses in ways that corrupt memory arbitrarily, not just produce a wrong-but-bounded result. Safe Rust prevents this by construction through ownership transfer, the borrowing rules, and the Send/Sync bounds enforced at thread boundaries. Only unsafe code can reintroduce a data race, which is why those accesses must be synchronized with atomics or locks.

reviewAnswers.question: What is the difference between a raw pointer and a reference in terms of promises made to the optimizer?
reviewAnswers.answer: A raw pointer is just an address with no promises attached: it may be null, dangling, misaligned, or aliased, which is exactly why creating one and doing arithmetic on it is always safe while dereferencing it is not. A reference is an address plus a contract the optimizer relies on: &T promises the pointee is valid, aligned, and immutable for the reference's lifetime, and &mut T additionally promises exclusive access with no other live reference to the same data. The optimizer uses those promises to cache loads, reorder, and assume no aliasing. Turning a raw pointer back into a reference reintroduces all of those promises, so the conversion is sound only if they genuinely hold.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is `MaybeUninit<T>` the right model for not-yet-valid storage?
reviewAnswers.answer: Uninitialized memory is not a valid value of any type, and reading it as a real T is undefined behavior; the same applies to constructing invalid bit patterns for types with invariants such as references, bool, and many enums. MaybeUninit<T> models the not-yet-valid state explicitly: it reserves correctly sized and aligned storage without claiming a valid T lives there, and it suppresses drop glue so a partial value is never destructed. You write every required field or element, then call assume_init exactly once to assert that a valid T now exists. This makes the invalid state visible in the type system instead of hiding it behind a fake placeholder value, which is what keeps the one-way initialization ratchet honest.

reviewAnswers.question: When should an API be `unsafe fn` instead of a safe function with internal unsafe code?
reviewAnswers.answer: Keep the public API safe and isolate the unsafe internally when the callee can actually enforce the whole contract, for example a slice wrapper or parser that can check bounds, maintain ownership, and guarantee non-aliasing through an exclusive &mut borrow. Mark the function unsafe fn when correctness depends on facts only the caller can establish, such as a raw pointer being valid for a chosen lifetime or a caller-controlled aliasing guarantee that no runtime check can recover. The deciding question is whether the function can validate its preconditions itself; if it cannot, a safe signature would be asserting a guarantee it has no way to uphold, so the obligation must be pushed to the caller and documented precisely with a SAFETY contract.
